level1.name: Initial
level1.description: SMA seeks to adopt enterprise-wide planning and architectural frameworks to improve program delivery. Current processes are unstructured, reactive, and inconsistent.

level2.name: Developing
level2.description: SMA complies with federal regulations and guidance and has begun adopting MES industry-recognized planning and architectural frameworks. Although basic processes and systems exist, they are not fully standardized or documented. The SMA collects and reports state-specific and MES metrics as well as performance data.

level3.name: Defined
level3.description: SMA complies with federal regulations and guidance and has fully implemented MES industry-recognized planning and architectural frameworks. Processes, systems, and strategies are standardized, well-documented, and aligned across the organization. The SMA actively monitors and analyzes state-specific and MES metrics as well as performance data for improvements.

level4.name: Managed
level4.description: SMA maintains compliance, follows industry-recognized planning and architectural frameworks, and monitors MES performance to meet goals. Processes are fully operational, consistent, and well executed. The SMA actively monitors and analyzes state-specific and MES metrics as well as performance data for improvements. The organization is a thought-leader in the MES ecosystem and actively collaborates and shares approaches with other SMAs.

level5.name: Optimized
level5.description: The SMA employs advanced, data-driven strategies to manage MES planning and architecture to align predictive decision-making with the SMA's long-term goals. Integrated processes, technologies, and data drive enterprise optimization. The SMA's institutionalized innovation supports adaptability, scalability, and continuous improvement. The organization is nationally recognized and actively collaborates and shares solutions with other SMAs.

notApplicable.name: Not Applicable
notApplicable.description: Not applicable was added by request of SMAs during listening sessions in late 2024. SMAs noted that some maturity criteria are inapplicable to their business operations or MES.

businessArchitecture.name: Business Architecture
businessArchitecture.description: The business processes performed to deliver the capability.

aspects.name: Business Process Performance
aspects.description: To what extent is the performance of business processes supporting this capability consistently measured, monitored, and managed using meaningful metrics?

level1.description:
Business processes that support the capability are identified and defined, but performance expectations are implicit and not formally measured.
Process outcomes vary and are not consistently reviewed.

level2.description:
Business processes are documented in SOPs, including steps and accountable roles.
Performance expectations are understood informally but are not yet measured or tracked.

level3.description:
Business processes are standardized and executed consistently across the organization. All staff follow the same documented process steps, and processes are centrally accessible through a Business Process Catalog.
Process performance is not yet routinely measured, monitored, or reported using defined metrics.

level4.description:
Business processes have defined performance metrics (e.g., timeliness, quality, efficiency) that are regularly tracked, monitored, and reported. Process performance insights are used to identify bottlenecks and manage outcomes. Select steps may be automated to improve performance predictability.
Continuous optimization, trend analysis, feedback loops, and broader innovation are not yet fully institutionalized.
evidence: Performance metrics developed for defined outcomes

level5.description: Business process performance is continuously assessed and optimized using metrics, trends, and feedback. Data-driven insights are used to proactively improve effectiveness, efficiency, and capability outcomes through refinement, automation, and innovation.

aspects.name: Business Process Documentation
aspects.description: To what extent are the business processes that support this capability identified, documented using defined standards, centrally managed, and regularly maintained?

level1.description:
Business processes that support the capability are partially or inconsistently identified. Process documentation is incomplete, informal, or outdated.
Business process models (BPMs) are not fully developed or consistently used to guide execution.
evidence: Partial lists of processes supporting the capability
High level or informal process diagrams
Draft or outdated BPM with gaps
Reliance on institutional knowledge to understand processes

level2.description:
All business processes supporting the capability are fully identified and documented. BPMs are developed for each process and are available for staff reference, but modeling quality and consistency may vary.
Documentation standards may be limited or informal, and process models may not yet follow a common enterprise standard.
evidence: Complete inventory of processes mapped to capabilities
BPMs available for all supporting processes
Process documentation used for onboarding or training

level3.description:
Business processes supporting the capability are formally defined and documented using a common modeling standard (e.g., Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0 or organization-defined conventions), ensuring clarity, consistency, and adherence to industry best practices.
Process documentation may not yet be centrally managed in a standardized modeling tool with version control, traceability, and formal relationships to capabilities and metrics.
evidence: BPMs compliant with BPMN 2.0 or internal standards
Periodic BPM quality or compliance assessments

level4.description:
Business process documentation is managed in a standardized modeling tool that supports version control, change history, and traceability. Process models are maintained in an enterprise business process catalog with defined relationships to capabilities and metrics.
Process documentation updates may not yet be consistently driven by performance metrics, improvement insights, capability changes, or strategic priorities.
evidence: Version history and change logs for BPMs
Documented relationships between processes, capabilities, and metrics

level5.description:
BPMs follow a documented review schedule with clear ownership. Updates are driven by performance metrics, operational insights, and lessons learned, not ad-hoc changes. All changes are logged in Process improvement logs or formal change requests, ensuring traceability from issue identification through approval and implementation.
BPM updates are explicitly tied to changes in business capabilities, strategic priorities, or regulatory requirements, keeping process design current and strategically aligned.
evidence: Evidence of updates driven by metrics or insights
Process improvement logs or change requests
Alignment of BPM updates with capability or strategy changes

aspects.name: Business Process Governance
aspects.description: Are specific individuals assigned to process governance roles, and do they actively participate in governing the business processes that support this capability?

level1.description:
Process governance roles and responsibilities have not been established or assigned to individuals for the business processes that support the capability.
There is no clear accountability for process ownership, decision-making, or process governance.

level2.description:
Process governance roles and responsibilities for the business processes supporting the capability have been identified and assigned to individuals (e.g., capability/business owner, process owner), and key process terms, definitions, and acronyms used to support the capability have been identified and documented.
Assigned individuals may not yet consistently participate in process governance decisions or manage process changes and standards.
evidence: Process model view with roles identified
Documentation of key process terms, definitions, and acronyms used to support the capability

level3.description:
The SMA monitors the assignment of process governance roles to ensure minimal vacancy, and the assigned individuals actively participate in governing the business processes, including decision-making related to process changes, standards, and alignment to the capability.
Governance information may not yet be centrally stored, searchable, or accessible through an enterprise repository. Stakeholders may still have limited visibility into governed processes, role assignments, and process definitions.
evidence: Decisions documented with key decision makers noted

level4.description:
Process governance role assignments, process definitions, and key terms are stored in a central enterprise repository (e.g., business architecture or process catalog) and are accessible to stakeholders to search, discover, and understand the processes governed by the SMA.
Process governance may not yet be regularly assessed against enterprise outcomes, policies, standards, and methodologies. Continuous governance improvement may not yet be fully institutionalized.

level5.description: Business processes adhere to enterprise process governance outcomes, policies, standards, and methodologies and are regularly assessed to identify opportunities to improve process governance, effectiveness, and alignment with the supported capability.

aspects.name: Business Process Automation
aspects.description: To what extent are business processes that support this capability deliberately designed, automated, governed, measured, and continuously improved?

level1.description:
Business Process automation is minimal or nonexistent.
Processes supporting the capability are largely manual, with heavy reliance on spreadsheets, email, and individual workarounds.

level2.description:
Isolated or tactical automation exists for parts of the process, often using basic tools or scripts. Automation efforts are reactive and focused on local efficiency rather than end-to-end capability support.
Limited standards, reuse, or governance are applied.
evidence: Use of scripts, or  applications with limited documentation

level3.description:
Automation is formally designed and standardized for key processes supporting the capability. Common tools and platforms are adopted, processes are mapped prior to automation, and automation follows defined patterns. Documentation, roles, and controls are established.
Automation is not centrally governed, measured, monitored, or integrated across the full capability. Exception handling, lifecycle management, and performance reporting may not yet be mature.

level4.description:
Automation is centrally governed, measured, and integrated across the capability. End-to-end processes are automated where appropriate, with performance metrics, monitoring, exception handling, and lifecycle management in place. Automation reliably supports business outcomes.
Automation is not yet continuously optimized through advanced technologies, predictive insights, feedback loops, or innovation-focused improvement practices.

level5.description: Automation is continuously optimized and intelligent. Advanced technologies (e.g., Robotic process automation, orchestration, low-code, Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning) are leveraged to improve speed, quality, and adaptability. Data-driven insights and continuous feedback loops drive ongoing capability enhancement and innovation.

aspects.name: Business Process Reporting
aspects.description: Are the reports that are created to support this process documented and traceable to the specific data used to create each report?

level1.description:
Reports and measures that are produced to support this process have not been identified and documented.
There is no reliable basis for report governance or quality assessment.

level2.description:
Reports and measures that are produced to support this process have been identified and documented.
Consistent implementation may not yet be established.

level3.description:
Reports and measure standards have been established and implemented and are delivered to key stakeholders to support this process.
Detailed measure specifications and report definitions are not yet documented and traced to underlying information assets.

level4.description:
Detailed measure specifications and report definitions have been documented and are tracked to the impacted information used to produce the measure and report in a central metadata repository.
Reports and measures do not yet fully adhere to enterprise business intelligence standards, procedures, metadata requirements, and technology.
Regular quality assessment and improvement is yet to be fully institutionalized.

level5.description: Reports and measures that are used to support this process adhere to enterprise business intelligence processes, procedures, standards, metadata and technology and are regularly assessed to improve the quality of the reports and measures.

technology.name: Technology
technology.description: The technology infrastructure and application architecture supporting the capability.

subDimensions.name: Technical Infrastructure Management
subDimensions.description: Assess the Technical Architecture maturity of the Medicaid Enterprise System (MES).

aspects.name: Compute and Storage
aspects.description: Does the Medicaid Enterprise System have servers on premise, hybrid, or cloud with routine, scheduled backup?

level1.description:
The MES runs on physical servers with no virtualization, no automation, and no defined backup schedule.
Storage and backups are handled ad hoc and manually, with no consistent process for capacity planning or recovery.

level2.description:
The MES uses some virtualization, and storage and backups are performed on a defined schedule.
However, servers are still provisioned manually, configurations are not standardized, and there is no automation to manage growth or enforce consistency.

level3.description:
The majority of the MES runs in cloud environments, with resources provisioned through standard configurations and scripting and backups automated.
Governance over those configurations is not yet formalized, and storage growth, retention, and cost are not actively managed against defined thresholds.

level4.description:
The MES operates in cloud environments governed through standardized processes, with automation managing storage and backups for growth, volume, and retention.
Backups are not yet immutable by default, and cost and capacity thresholds are not formally defined or reviewed on a regular cadence.
evidence: Documentation of reviews and decisions made

level5.description:
The MES runs on cloud compute and hosting infrastructure across environments, with immutable backups retained per a defined schedule and compute and storage usage governed by cost and capacity thresholds that are regularly reviewed.
There are no manual provisioning dependencies, no ungoverned configurations, and no unmonitored consumption — capacity, cost, and recoverability are continuously managed.

aspects.name: Networking and Technical Recovery
aspects.description: Does the MES have network segmentation that is regularly tested for outages and recovery?

level1.description: The MES operates on a flat network with no segmentation and minimal traffic visibility. There are no defined recovery objectives, no failover capability, and no proactive monitoring — outages are discovered only when users report them and resolved manually.

level2.description: The MES has basic segmentation separating major workloads, and traffic logs are collected and reviewed periodically. Failover and restoration procedures exist but are not scheduled, not formally tracked, and not tied to defined recovery objectives, leaving recovery times unpredictable.
evidence: Technical Recovery Testing Schedule and results

level3.description: The MES network follows defined design patterns that segment workloads by sensitivity and function, and Recovery Time and Recovery Point Objectives are documented in Service Level Agreements (SLAs). However, monitoring is not continuous, anomaly detection is not in place, and testing is performed only initially rather than on an ongoing schedule.
evidence: Recovery Time Objective (RTO), Recovery Point Objective (RPO), SLAs

level4.description: The MES continuously monitors network traffic against established baselines with anomaly detection, enforces standardized network patterns through governance, and tests failover and restoration on a scheduled basis with SLA performance reported and consistently met. Failover and remediation, however, are not yet automated and still require manual intervention, and the network is not designed around zero-trust principles.
evidence: Technical Recovery Testing Schedule and results

level5.description: The MES network applies micro-segmentation and zero-trust principles, with continuous observability and proactive optimization sustaining performance during peak demand. There are no manual recovery dependencies, no untested failure paths, and no unmonitored segments — automated failover, self-healing, and redundant environments deliver recovery with little to no user impact, validated through regular resilience exercises.

aspects.name: Identity, Access and Consent
aspects.description: Does the MES have identity, access, and consent services for internal and external users?

level1.description: The MES has limited ability to manage user identity and access, with no centralized system and no role-based controls. Consent for Medicaid applicants and members is captured manually, with no audit trail and no defined process for revocation.

level2.description: The MES has standardized identity and access management for new systems, and some applications capture consent from Medicaid applicants and members. However, legacy systems are not yet integrated, consent is not consistently captured across the MES, and revocation still requires manual intervention.
evidence: Identity management, verification, and access request process documentation

level3.description: The MES uses centralized identity and access management for most applications with Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), and Medicaid applicant and member consent, preferences, and revocation are collected and auditable within most applications. Coverage is not yet complete across all systems, and access activity is not consistently logged or centrally managed.
evidence: RBAC documentation, identity management architecture diagram

level4.description: The MES uses centralized identity and access management with RBAC across all applications, and access activities are logged and auditable. Medicaid applicant and member consent, preferences, and revocation are centrally managed, though they are not yet user-managed or shared across external systems and partner organizations.

level5.description: The MES integrates identity and access management across internal and external systems and organizations, with continuous improvement and automation governing access decisions. There are no siloed identity stores, no manually tracked consent records, and no barriers to revocation — Medicaid applicant and member consent, preferences, and revocation are user-managed and shared seamlessly across internal and external MES systems and Medicaid organizations.

aspects.name: Security Protection and Monitoring
aspects.description: Does the MES have security controls, with incident logging and monitoring?

level1.description: The MES applies security controls inconsistently across systems, with no enforced standards. Monitoring is limited, alerting is minimal, and there is no centralized visibility into security events, leaving gaps where threats can go undetected.

level2.description: The MES has security controls defined and partially implemented across applications. Monitoring exists but alerts are reviewed manually, with no automation, no consistent coverage across all systems, and no formal process for measuring control effectiveness.

level3.description: The MES has security controls implemented across Medicaid applications, with data encrypted in transit and at rest, and monitoring and logs reviewed on a regular cadence. Reviews are not yet automated, auditing is not continuous, and incident detection still depends on manual analysis.

level4.description: The MES has consistently implemented security controls with regular auditing, automated control checks, and automated alerting on security events and incidents. Controls are not yet continuously optimized, validation against evolving threats is periodic rather than ongoing, and the program is not yet positioned to exceed baseline regulatory expectations.

level5.description: The MES has security controls that are continuously optimized, audited, and validated, with monitoring fully supporting compliance and audit readiness. There are no unmonitored systems, no unreviewed controls, and no reactive-only processes — the security posture is proactive, evidence-based, and consistently exceeds federal and state regulatory expectations.
evidence: Security control inventory and monitoring logs

aspects.name: System Operations and Monitoring
aspects.description: Does the MES have SOPs and performance monitoring?

level1.description: The MES is operated manually with limited documentation, and system logs are reviewed reactively for performance issues. There are no defined procedures, no monitoring standards, and no proactive alerting, leaving operations dependent on individual knowledge.

level2.description: The MES is operated manually with partial documentation of processes and procedures, and basic guidelines exist for monitoring performance. Procedures are not yet consistently followed, service levels are not formally defined, and monitoring is not tied to automated alerting.
evidence: System operations documentation, SLAs with metrics
Monitoring and alerting rules, documentation, and diagrams

level3.description: The MES operates according to documented internal procedures with defined SLAs, and monitoring and alerting cover application performance and health. Procedures are internally defined rather than aligned to industry standards, automation is limited, and alerting is not yet integrated with broader systems operations.
evidence: Documentation showing operations align with industry-standard processes
Documentation of monitoring and alerting integrated with systems operations

level4.description: The MES operates following industry-standard processes, with automation applied where feasible and monitoring and alerting integrated with systems operations. Performance is not yet benchmarked against external standards, continuous improvement is not formalized, and analytics across operational data are not centralized.
evidence: Centralized operational analytics for performance and health
System operations documentation with SLA and metrics
Monitoring and alerting rules, documentation, and diagrams

level5.description: The MES operations are benchmarked against industry standards and continuously improved, with centralized monitoring and alerting analytics providing a unified view of application performance and health. There are no undocumented procedures, no manual operations where automation is feasible, and no siloed monitoring — operations are proactive, data-driven, and continuously refined.

aspects.name: Development, Testing, Release and Security Compliance
aspects.description: Does the MES have centralized source and script management with testing and security reviews?

level1.description: The MES has no version control of source code or scripts, testing is performed manually, and security compliance checks are limited or absent. Changes are released infrequently as large, all-at-once updates, with no traceability, no iterative delivery, and no feedback loop between development and the people who use the system.

level2.description: The MES has basic version control of source code and scripts, releases and testing follow checklists, and security compliance reviews are performed manually. Changes are still integrated and released in large, infrequent batches, testing is not automated, and slow feedback cycles limit the team's ability to deliver and adjust incrementally.
evidence: Records from prior application security testing

level3.description: The MES has standardized version control with pre-production environments and documented release, testing, and security review procedures. Developers integrate changes into a shared codebase on a regular cadence and deliver work in smaller increments, though integration and testing are not yet automated, batch sizes remain larger than ideal, and feedback to teams is not yet fast or continuous.
evidence: Standardized release and testing process documentation
Version control / branching and integration strategy documentation

level4.description: The MES has centralized version control with automated build, testing, and release pipelines across pre-production environments, and security reviews are integrated into release planning. Small, incremental changes are delivered on a regular cadence with automated regression testing providing fast feedback to teams. Releases to production are not yet continuous, and post-release monitoring is not yet ongoing.
evidence: Automated release workflow / pipeline configuration documentation
Automated test coverage and regression results
Evidence of security reviews integrated into release planning

level5.description: The MES has fully automated source code and script management with continuous integration and continuous delivery across pre-production and production environments, monitored deployments, and continuous security and compliance validation. The pipeline supports rapid, iterative response to changing requirements with little to no manual intervention. There are no large-batch releases, and no untested changes reaching production— development operates as a continuous, feedback-driven, and secure pipeline.
evidence: Comprehensive development, configuration, and release process documentation
CI/CD pipeline and release workflow documentation

subDimensions.name: Application Management
subDimensions.description: Assess the Technical Architecture maturity of the application or module for a Domain/Area's capability.

aspects.name: API, Messaging, and Integration
aspects.description: Does the Medicaid application connect and interface with other internal or external systems or organizations?

level1.description: The MES application or module connects to other systems for a single, limited purpose using an API, interface, or manual batch file exchange, with limited documentation. There is no inventory of connections, no defined standards, and no governance over how external integrations are established or maintained.
evidence: Basic description of the connection or interface
Description of the data exchanged and with which system

level2.description: The MES application or module connects through an API, interface, or scheduled batch file exchange that is documented and tracked in an inventory. Connections do not yet follow industry standards, there is no consistent process for establishing new integrations, and event-driven patterns are not in use.
evidence: Interface specifications and batch exchange schedules

level3.description: The MES application or module uses APIs or interfaces that follow industry standards, and all external connections are established through a documented process. APIs are not yet centrally managed or versioned, integrations are not event-driven, and there is no automated way to publish or discover available services.
evidence: Documented process for establishing external connections
API specifications aligned to industry standards

level4.description: The MES application or module uses APIs or interfaces that are event-driven where appropriate, published and versioned through an API management tool, and consistently apply industry standards. Conformance with standards is not yet fully validated, integrations are not continuously optimized, and external connection management is not yet fully automated.
evidence: API catalog or registry from an API management tool

level5.description: The MES application or module uses APIs or interfaces that fully conform with industry standards, are continuously optimized through automated adjustments, and have all external connections actively managed. There are no undocumented integrations, no manual file exchanges where APIs are feasible, and no unmonitored connections — interoperability is standards-based, fully governed, and continuously refined.
evidence: Documentation of automated monitoring and optimization
External connection management and oversight records

aspects.name: Application Hosting and Platform Services
aspects.description: Is the Medicaid application hosted in a dedicated MES environment with common platform services reused?

level1.description: The MES application or module is hosted in an environment with limited documentation and inconsistent configurations. There are no defined hosting standards, no shared services, and no consistency across environments, making the hosting setup difficult to support or replicate.

level2.description: The MES application or module is hosted in a documented environment, with standardization of MES hosting practices being piloted. Standards are not yet broadly adopted, common services are not available across applications, and configurations still vary between environments.

level3.description: The MES application or module is hosted in an environment that adopts and follows standard hosting patterns, with some common services available across the MES. Standards are not yet enforced to reduce complexity, automation is limited, and resources are not shared across hosting environments.
evidence: Catalog of common or shared services

level4.description: The MES application or module is hosted in an environment that applies standards to limit complexity, supports automation, and shares resources across MES hosting environments. Hosting is not yet proactively managed, automation is not used to optimize performance and reliability, and resource reuse is not yet widespread.

level5.description: The MES application or module is hosted in an environment that is proactively managed, uses automation to continuously improve application performance and reliability, and reuses resources widely across MES hosting environments. There are no undocumented configurations, no isolated or duplicated services, and no reactive-only management — hosting is standardized, automated, and continuously optimized.
evidence: Proactive hosting management and monitoring documentation
Documentation of automated performance and reliability optimization
Shared resource reuse catalog and reporting

aspects.name: Business Rules and Workflows
aspects.description: Does the Medicaid application enable and support SMA business processes?

level1.description: The MES application or module has business rules and workflows that are hard coded into source code and require technical staff to change. There is no documentation, no separation between rules and code, and no ability for business users to understand or influence how rules operate.

level2.description: The MES application or module has business rules and workflows that remain hard-coded but are documented for internal use by technical staff. Documentation is not in a business-readable format, rules are not separated from code, and changes still depend entirely on technical resources.
evidence: Technical documentation of business rules and workflows for internal use

level3.description: The MES application or module has business rules and workflows documented in a human-readable format and maintained separately from scripts or code. Rules are not yet externalized from the application itself, are not reused across modules, and still require code changes to update.
evidence: Business rules documented in a human-readable format
Documentation showing rules maintained separately from code

level4.description: The MES application or module has business rules and workflows externalized from scripts or source code and reused across multiple applications or modules. Rules are not yet versioned across the MES, governance over reuse is informal, and updates are not driven by automation.
evidence: Documentation of rules reused across applications or modules
Business rules engine or configuration documentation

level5.description: The MES application or module has business rules and workflows that are fully externalized, versioned, and reused across the MES, with adjustments made through policy-informed automation. There are no hard-coded rules, no duplicated logic across modules, and no purely manual rule changes — business rules are managed as a governed, reusable asset.
evidence: Governance documentation for reuse across the MES

aspects.name: Modular Architecture
aspects.description: Can the Medicaid application and its services be changed or updated without impacting the system?

level1.description: The MES application or module is a large, complex system where changes require system-level updates. There are no independently deployable services, no separation of common functions, and no ability to modify one capability without affecting the broader system.

level2.description: The MES application or module has identified some services as candidates for modularity. Those services are not yet separated from the core application, cannot be deployed independently, and are not reused by other modules.

level3.description: The MES application or module has common services that can be deployed independently of the application or module. Those services are not yet reused across other MES applications, redundancy still exists between modules, and there is no broader composability strategy.

level4.description: The MES application or module has common services that are reused by other MES applications and modules to reduce redundancy. The system is not yet fully composable, services are not all discrete, and changes to individual capabilities can still require coordinated updates across modules.

level5.description: The MES application or module is fully composable, with discrete services that allow independent and adaptive changes. There are no monolithic dependencies, no duplicated services across modules, and no system-level updates required for capability changes — the architecture supports independent evolution of each service.

aspects.name: User Interfaces and Session Management
aspects.description: Does the Medicaid application have standardized user interfaces, responsive design, accessibility testing, and maintain SMA user progress?

level1.description: The MES application or module has user interfaces that are inconsistently designed with limited accessibility support, and user progress is not maintained between sessions. There are no usability standards, no accessibility testing, and no mechanism for users to save or resume their work.
evidence: Presence or lack of user persistence

level2.description: The MES application or module has some standardization of user interfaces and has conducted limited usability testing, with basic ability to maintain user progress. Standards are not yet applied consistently, accessibility testing is not formalized, and user feedback is not systematically collected.

level3.description: The MES application or module has standardized user interfaces, collects user feedback to inform planned improvements, and allows users to resume their progress. Designs are not yet fully responsive across devices and browsers, accessibility testing is not automated, and progress is not maintained across multiple devices.
evidence: Application documentation, user session management pattern documentation

level4.description: The MES application or module has responsive design across different devices and browsers, automated accessibility testing in place, and users can maintain progress across devices. Personalization is not supported, user feedback is not yet driving continuous improvement, and sessions are not context-aware across channels.
evidence: Application frontend documentation, User interface documentation and standards
Automated accessibility testing procedures and results
Application documentation, user session management pattern documentation

level5.description: The MES application or module supports user interface personalization, uses ongoing user feedback to continuously improve the front-end experience, and preserves user sessions in a context-aware way across devices and browsers. There are no inconsistent designs, no untested accessibility gaps, and no lost user context — the experience is personalized, accessible, and continuously refined.
evidence: Application frontend design standards and reusable components
Automated accessibility testing procedures and results
Application documentation, user session management pattern documentation

outcomes.name: Organizational Outcomes
outcomes.description: The definition of the desired outcomes that require the capability to be achieved. (Optional)

aspects.name: Culture & Mindset
aspects.description: To what extent are organizational norms, expectations, and behaviors related to outcome development?

level1.description: No culture or expectation of outcomes for projects (at any phase of the project).

level2.description: Recognition begins to take hold of the importance of outcomes during planning.

level3.description: Leadership sets expectations: outcome development during planning becomes a norm.

level4.description: Outcome development is formalized and institutionally expected.

level5.description: Outcome thinking is fully embedded at all levels of organization—without direction by or requirement from leadership.

aspects.name: Capability
aspects.description: To what extent is there internal capacity to develop, oversee, and apply outcomes without reliance on vendors?

level1.description: No internal capabilities to identify or draft outcomes.

level2.description: Organization understands at a high-level what elements are needed to identify and draft outcomes, but vendor leads development of outcomes.

level3.description: Sufficient experience in identifying and drafting outcomes internally; organization may lead or closely oversee vendors to draft outcomes.

level4.description: Full in-house capability to independently produce outcomes.

level5.description:
Deep in-house expertise with fully self-sufficient teams across the organization.
Organization may also support sister organizations and agencies in developing outcomes.

aspects.name: Quality & Consistency
aspects.description: To what extent is there clarity, structure, and strategic alignment of outcome statements?

level1.description: Outcomes are ambiguous, inconsistent, and disconnected from goals.

level2.description:
No consistent approach or methodology to developing outcomes.
Outcomes may be aligned with priorities but are not “smart” or actionable.

level3.description:
Defined approach or methodology to developing outcomes.
Outcomes capture the capability sought and benefit derived from a given project, but the quality of the outcome statements vary.

level4.description:
Well-established and consistently applied approach to developing outcomes.
Outcomes are clear, actionable, reusable, and strategically aligned.

level5.description:
Well-established and consistently applied approach to developing outcomes.
Outcome statements are of consistently high quality, recognizable, and standardized.

aspects.name: Alignment to Goals & Priorities
aspects.description: To what extent are outcomes traceable to broader goals, priorities, and mission?

level1.description: Outcomes are not aligned to goals or priorities.

level2.description: Emerging awareness of need to align outcomes with goals and priorities but gaps remain.

level3.description: Outcomes are intentionally aligned to strategic goals and priorities.

level4.description:
Systematic alignment of outcomes to goals and priorities.
Outcomes inform broader strategies.

level5.description: Outcomes reflect and reinforce strategic direction seamlessly.

aspects.name: Use of Metrics
aspects.description: To what extent are outcomes tracked, and metrics used to measure progress and guide improvement?

level1.description: No recognition of the need to measure progress toward achieving outcomes or commitment to continuous improvement.

level2.description:
Interest in measuring progress toward achieving outcomes.
Metrics are not well-aligned with outcomes.

level3.description:
Metrics are generally appropriate and regularly referenced to determine progress in achieving outcomes.
Some engagement in continuous improvement cycles.

level4.description:
Metrics are well-developed.
Staff regularly use metrics to evaluate performance and engage in well-established continuous improvement cycles.

level5.description:
Performance monitoring is deeply embedded in organization's culture.
Metrics and outcomes support continuous improvement, learning, and decision-making.

aspects.name: Reusability & Integration
aspects.description: To what extent are outcomes reused across project documents, Advance Planning Documents (APD), systems, and reporting?

level1.description:
No reuse.
Outcomes are informal or nonexistent.

level2.description: Reuse is isolated to APDs; no reuse across other projects, planning, or leadership documents.

level3.description:
Reuse is focused on APDs and some project-related documents.
Inconsistent reuse across leadership documents, and external communications.

level4.description: Reuse is consistent and intentional across APDs, project documents, and leadership and external communications.

level5.description: Seamless reuse across systems and communications, which improves coherence and efficiency.

roles.name: Organizational Roles
roles.description: The individual roles responsible for providing the capability. (Optional)

aspects.name: Organizational Goals Alignment
aspects.description: To what extent do organizational goals align around shared, enterprise-wide Medicaid goals?

level1.description: Business units operate in silos without clear understanding of enterprise-wide Medicaid goals.

level2.description: Organizational goals are defined but not fully communicated across all levels.

level3.description: Business units align their roles and processes to support broader Medicaid goals.

level4.description: All roles (internal and external) collaborate to drive enterprise-wide Medicaid program goals, with regular reassessments for alignment.

level5.description: SMA leadership collaborates at the national level to set adaptable, data-driven goals and performance outcomes for the Medicaid program; focus is on improving healthcare and social services delivery and beneficiary well-being nationwide.

aspects.name: Governance & Standardization
aspects.description: To what extent does governance support data-driven solutions and standardization of processes which are shared more broadly?

level1.description: Limited or no formal governance to guide roles or standardize processes.

level2.description: Some governance exists, but role clarity and process standardization are inconsistent.

level3.description: Formal governance structures support role clarity, with standard operating procedures (SOPs).

level4.description: Enterprise governance bodies actively coordinate roles, processes, and data for continuous improvement and standardization.

level5.description: SMA leads data-driven solutions at a national level and collaborates with other SMAs to develop shared business and technical standards that are disseminated nationally to strengthen overall Medicaid service delivery.

aspects.name: Communication (Internal / External)
aspects.description: To what extent is communication integrated across business areas to support Medicaid goals and outcomes?

level1.description: Minimal communication between leadership, business, and technical units.

level2.description: Defined communication channels exist but are not used consistently.

level3.description: Regular cross-unit communication occurs, including with external partners like Managed Care Organizations (MCO) and vendors.

level4.description: Transparent, enterprise-wide communication ensures all roles understand priorities, responsibilities, and impacts.

level5.description:
Integrates communication across all business areas to align long-term Medicaid goals and performance outcomes.
Fosters cooperation with other SMAs, CMS, and external partners nationally.
The Agency is recognized for its leadership in sharing solutions, provider enrollment process needs, and best practices.

aspects.name: Culture & Leadership
aspects.description: To what extent does leadership support a culture of continuous learning and collaboration?

level1.description: Leadership lacks visibility into workloads and resource capacity; roles are reactive.

level2.description: Leadership begins assessing role capacity but lacks full enterprise insight.

level3.description: Leadership proactively manages workloads and roles based on enterprise needs and priorities.

level4.description: Leadership fosters a culture of collaboration and continuous learning across internal and external roles.

level5.description: Leadership supports internal change agents to align culture, strategy, and resources with long-term Medicaid goals.

aspects.name: Resourcing Capacity (Staffing, Training, Recruitment)
aspects.description: How are staffing, training, and recruitment processes identified and aligned with program objectives?

level1.description: SMA struggles to identify gaps in role capacity; staffing is reactive.

level2.description: Some processes exist for role capacity management (staffing, training, recruitment).

level3.description: SMA systematically identifies, recruits, and trains staff.

level4.description: SMA maintains a dynamic capacity model to forecast and meet enterprise role needs, including succession planning and continuous role development.

level5.description: SMA uses comprehensive planning and advanced analytics to align roles and skills with program objectives, enabling rapid response to required changes while maintaining high service delivery standards.

enterprise-architecture.name: Organizational Enterprise Architecture
enterprise-architecture.description: Assesses the organization's maturity in enterprise-level planning, governance, and architectural frameworks across the Medicaid enterprise.

aspects.name: Business Capability
aspects.description: How clearly are business capabilities described and documented, managed, measured, and regularly improved so they effectively support the enterprise?

level1.description:
The capability has been identified, and the use of the capability has been documented.
The capability is not yet fully described across roles, processes, technology, information, or performance measures. Compliance alignment may not yet be fully documented.

level2.description:
Documentation of the capability roles, supporting processes, technology, and information has begun. The capability complies with state and federal requirements.
Capability documentation is in progress but is not yet complete or standardized. Performance measures may still be under development, and enterprise alignment may not yet be established.

level3.description:
Capability roles, supporting processes, technology and information are fully defined and documented. The capability complies with state and federal requirements and the conforms to MES industry - recognized architectural frameworks. The capability is standardized and aligned at the enterprise level.
The capability is defined and standardized, but performance is not yet actively managed or routinely monitored through metrics.

level4.description:
The SMA manages the capability for performance and compliance. Metrics and measures of the capability are monitored.
The capability is monitored and managed, but performance data may not yet be consistently used to drive improvements, investment decisions, or cross-SMA thought leadership.

level5.description: The SMA uses performance monitoring to make improvements to the capability. The SMA is a thought leader for the capability and shares capability information with other SMAs.
evidence: Advance Planning Document (APD) showing improvement or investment in the advancement or improvement of the capability

aspects.name: Enterprise Architecture
aspects.description: To what extent is enterprise architecture (EA) integrated into MITA enterprise planning, governance, and execution to guide and optimize business, information, and technology outcomes?

level1.description:
Recognition of the need for enterprise-wide planning and architectural frameworks but current EA practices are not structured, standardized, or consistently applied.
Planning is reactive, and architectural guidance is inconsistent across the enterprise.

level2.description:
Compliance with federal guidance and adoption of MES-recognized EA frameworks. EA processes exist but are not standardized or fully documented.
EA may still be compliance-driven rather than integrated into planning and execution.

level3.description:
Fully implemented MES-recognized EA frameworks. EA processes are standardized, documented, and aligned across business, information and technology.
EA is not yet consistently used to actively monitor MES performance, manage outcomes, or guide strategic execution.

level4.description:
EA is used to monitor and manage MES performance. EA is integrated into strategic planning and execution. SMA collaborates with other SMAs to share EA practices.
EA may not yet be fully data-driven, predictive, or continuously optimized. National-level leadership and proactive enterprise optimization are not yet demonstrated.

level5.description: Advanced, data-driven EA is used as strategies for proactive decision-making. EA drives enterprise optimization and continuous improvement. SMA is nationally recognized for enterprise architecture leadership.

aspects.name: Policy Management
aspects.description: To what extent are policies systematically integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide compliance, decision-making, and execution within MITA?

level1.description:
Policies relevant to business capabilities are informally identified or inconsistently documented.
There is little to no mapping of policies to business processes or systems.

level2.description:
Some policies are documented and work has begun to map to business processes and systems. Compliance is mostly reactive, and regular reviews are not established.
Policies are not yet fully integrated into governance, planning, or execution.

level3.description:
All business policies relevant to the capability (e.g., "Pharmacy Management") are identified, documented, and mapped to business processes and supporting systems. Policies are harmonized with state and federal requirements, and their alignment is regularly reviewed to ensure compliance and support for enterprise objectives.
Policy alignment is not yet fully institutionalized across enterprise governance. Policy updates may not yet be consistently driven by performance data, regulatory change, or strategic objectives.

level4.description:
Policy alignment is institutionalized and integrated into enterprise governance. Policies are systematically reviewed, updated, and optimized based on performance data, regulatory changes, and strategic objectives.
Policy alignment may not yet function as a fully proactive, continuous driver of agility, innovation, and external thought leadership.

level5.description: Policy alignment is a proactive, continuous process that drives organizational agility, compliance, and innovation. The organization demonstrates thought leadership and collaborates externally to share best practices.

aspects.name: Strategic Planning
aspects.description: To what extent is strategic planning formally integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide the execution of MITA?

level1.description:
Strategic plan is informally considered during architecture and capability planning efforts.
Alignment between strategy and capabilities occurs opportunistically and is largely dependent on individual initiative rather than a defined planning approach.

level2.description:
Strategic plan and capability planning are intentionally aligned through defined outcomes. Strategic objectives inform capability discussions, but dependencies between strategy, capabilities, and processes are not yet consistently analyzed or governed.
Strategic alignment exists but may not yet drive portfolio or project prioritization.

level3.description:
Strategic plan explicitly identifies capabilities as required dependencies to achieve strategic outcomes. Capabilities and supporting processes are identified and analyzed as part of Enterprise Portfolio and Project Management to inform prioritization and planning decisions.
Capabilities and supporting processes are not yet consistently tied to roadmap execution, intake decisions, APD funding requests, or project approval processes.

level4.description:
Enterprise Roadmap (Projects/Initiatives) have capabilities and processes identified that support the roadmap items. Capabilities and processes are identified and analyzed for intake of new business to support funding requests for an APD, or state funding for project approval.
Capabilities and processes may not yet be fully institutionalized as core inputs to all enterprise governance, investment, and prioritization decisions.

level5.description: Capabilities and processes are core inputs to enterprise governance and decision-making. Strategic planning, investment decisions, and roadmap prioritization are consistently driven by capability and process analysis to ensure alignment, maximize value, and support execution of SMA strategic objectives.
